analysis.investment_thesis: Crompton is a classic Indian consumer electricals stalwart — steady market presence in fans, pumps, and appliances with a recovering profit trajectory — but the P/E of 34x on 10% revenue growth is a GARP violation I can't ignore. The story is sensible (India's rising consumer aspirations), but the price demands a faster-grower than this business actually is.
key_strengths: Virtually debt-free with D/E of 0.05 after aggressively paying down INR 1,686 Cr peak borrowings to INR 186 Cr by FY25
Consistent free cash flow generation — positive OCF all 5 years, FCF averaging ~INR 650 Cr annually
Strong institutional conviction with DII holding at 65.73%, suggesting domestic funds see long-term value in the franchise
key_risks: Revenue CAGR of 9.8% over 7 years is stalwart territory — far below the 15–20%+ I need to justify a 34x P/E
Net profit has been volatile and is only INR 564 Cr in FY25 — still below FY21's INR 617 Cr peak, suggesting limited earnings power expansion
Operating margin at 7.99% is thin for a consumer brand, leaving little cushion against commodity cost spikes or competitive pricing pressure
red_flags: PEG ratio of ~3.4x (P/E 34 / ~10% earnings growth) — nearly 3.5x my comfort threshold of 1.0
Net profit in FY25 (INR 564 Cr) is actually lower than FY21 (INR 617 Cr) despite 4 more years of business — no real earnings compounding over the mid-term
Finance costs spiked to INR 109 Cr in FY23 indicating the Butterfly brand acquisition added meaningful financial complexity; post-integration execution still unproven at scale
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Crompton is exactly the kind of business I'd spot while buying a ceiling fan — everyone has one, the brand is trusted, and India's housing and rural electrification boom should keep demand growing. The debt paydown story is genuinely impressive: from INR 1,686 Cr in FY22 to INR 186 Cr in FY25, and free cash flow has been reliably positive. The Butterfly kitchen appliances acquisition broadens the platform into a higher-growth segment.

The problem is price. At P/E 34x with earnings growing roughly 8–10% historically, the PEG is a punishing 3.4x. Even if I give credit to the forward P/E of 27x and assume 20% profit growth ahead (an optimistic scenario), the PEG is still ~1.35x. Operating margins at 8% leave little room for upside surprises. I'd want this stock in the low 20x range before getting excited — call it INR 175–190 — not here.
